title: The forgiveness of sins (CCC 976–983)
hook: the Catechism says there is no offense the Church cannot forgive

segments.voice: Yesterday, the laity: clergy, laypeople and religious, different callings in one people. Your line was equal dignity.

Near the end of the Apostles' Creed, after the Church and the communion of saints, comes a short line that's easy to say too fast: the forgiveness of sins. It sits right next to some very large claims, the resurrection of the body and life everlasting. That placement is a clue. The Creed doesn't treat forgiveness as a footnote for bad weeks. It puts it among the things a Catholic believes about how the whole world is put right.
screen: `A SHORT LINE, SAID FAST.` → `NEXT TO THE RESURRECTION.` → `NOT A FOOTNOTE.`

segments.voice: Back on day three, this path stepped into the confessional. Today, the line in the Creed behind it. On Easter evening, in John's Gospel, the disciples sit behind locked doors. Jesus stands among them, breathes on them, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Receive ye the Holy Ghost. Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them." The Catechism ties the Creed's line to that room: forgiveness belongs with the Spirit given to the apostles, and with the Church sent out with the power to forgive. Then the doorway. The Catechism calls baptism the first and chief sacrament of forgiveness. In baptism, Catholics believe, sins are washed away completely, and a person starts clean. Then the second chance. Baptism doesn't take away human weakness, the Catechism admits, and the clean start doesn't stay clean. So for sins after baptism it turns to the sacrament of penance, confession. In its later section on confession, it borrows an old picture from early Church writers: after a shipwreck, a plank to hold on to. Then the claim itself. There is no offense, however serious, that the Church cannot forgive. No one, however wicked, should doubt that forgiveness is possible, as long as they are truly sorry. This isn't a promise that sin doesn't count. It's a promise that sorrow is never too late. The Catechism adds that Christ wants the door of forgiveness always open to anyone who turns back. So the line in the Creed is less about bookkeeping than about hope: a life can be reopened.
screen: `RECEIVE YE THE HOLY GHOST.` · `BAPTISM, THE FIRST FORGIVENESS.` · `A PLANK AFTER THE SHIPWRECK.` · `NO OFFENSE TOO SERIOUS.`

segments.voice: Let one thing come to mind that still sits heavy, something you did or failed to do. Don't replay the story; name it quietly in a few words. If you pray, hand it over to God, and if you're Catholic, you might decide when you'll bring it to confession; if you don't pray, loosen your grip for these two minutes and let it be smaller than you are.

The forgiveness of sins. A line of the Creed, joined to the Spirit and the Church: given first in baptism, offered again in confession, and, the Catechism says, closed to no one who is truly sorry. Today's word.
Your line: no sin too big. No list of wrongs is too long for mercy to reach. Go gently.

howItsDone: Catholics profess the forgiveness of sins in the Creed at Mass, and seek forgiveness for sins after baptism in the sacrament of penance, confessing to a priest and receiving absolution.

chat.says: Does the Catholic Church really think any sin can be forgiven?
options: Yes. The Catechism says no offense is too serious for anyone who is truly sorry.
Only small ones; serious sins must be worked off before God will forgive them.
Yes, if you say the right prayer, even if you aren't sorry at all.

notes: The Catechism is not public domain; every CCC point is paraphrased (976 Creed links forgiveness to the Spirit and the Church; 977 baptism the first and chief sacrament of forgiveness; 980 penance after baptism, with the Fathers' 'plank after shipwreck' image; 982 no offense too serious, for anyone sincerely repentant; the door always open to anyone who turns back). Confirm each paraphrase, and that the shipwreck plank image is fairly placed here (the CCC uses it in this section and in 1446).
